slides.0.title: The vine and its annual cycle
slides.0.subtitle: From budburst to harvest: every stage can make or break a vintage
slides.1.title: Structure of the vine
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Roots, trunk and shoots
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Roots take up water and nutrients and store carbohydrates; the trunk and permanent arms support the canopy; each year shoots grow from buds, carrying leaves, tendrils and inflorescences
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Leaves: the photosynthesis factory
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Leaves use sunlight, CO₂ and water to make sugars that feed ripening and growth; the ratio of leaf area to fruit weight is key to whether the crop can ripen
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Composition of the berry
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Skins hold colour, tannin and aroma precursors; pulp holds water, sugar and acid; seeds hold coarser tannins. Many winemaking decisions are really about how much to extract from which part
slides.1.content: Know the plant and the berry first; every later decision builds on them.
slides.2.title: The annual growth cycle
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Budburst
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Buds open once average temperatures reach about 10°C; early-budding varieties and sites are most at risk from spring frost, which can destroy the primary buds for the year
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Flowering and fruit set
slides.2.highlights.1.content: After flowering, fertilised flowers develop into berries. Cold, rain or strong wind cause coulure (poor set) or millerandage (uneven berries), directly cutting yield
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Véraison and ripening
slides.2.highlights.2.content: At véraison berries soften and red varieties colour; then sugar rises, acidity falls and tannins and aromas mature. Late-summer and autumn weather decides whether this completes
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Dormancy
slides.2.highlights.3.content: After harvest leaves fall and the vine goes dormant, storing reserves; winter pruning sets next season’s bud number and so the starting point for yield. Extreme cold (as in the eastern US) can kill buds or even trunks
slides.2.content: Each stage has its matching risk: spring frost, poor fruit set, incomplete ripening, winter freeze.
slides.3.title: Ripeness: sugar, acid, phenolics and aroma
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Sugar and potential alcohol
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Sugar sets potential alcohol; in warm climates it accumulates fast, easily giving high alcohol
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Acidity
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Mainly tartaric and malic acid; malic acid falls quickly through respiration in heat, so warm-climate wines are lower in acid and cool-climate wines higher
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Phenolic ripeness
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Ripeness of tannins and pigments (browning seeds, softer tannins) does not always keep pace with sugar. With warming, sugar often arrives before phenolic ripeness: a new problem in many regions
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Aroma development
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Methoxypyrazines in unripe fruit give green pepper and grassy notes and fall with ripening and sunlight; riper fruit has richer fruit aromas. Choosing a harvest date is a trade-off between sugar, acid, phenolics and aroma
slides.3.content: The harvest-date decision is the most common link from viticulture to style in Diploma essays.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
At roughly what average temperature does the vine begin budburst?
A. About 20°C
B. About 30°C
C. About 0°C
D. About 10°C
About 10°C is the usual budburst threshold and the base for degree-day calculations.
What is the most likely result of cold, wet weather at flowering?
A. A big rise in sugar
B. Early véraison
C. Acidity falls to zero
D. Coulure and millerandage, lower yield
Poor fruit set directly reduces yield.
Why are warm-climate wines usually lower in acidity?
A. Tartaric acid turns into sugar
B. Malic acid falls quickly through respiration in heat
C. Acidification is banned in warm climates
D. Skins get thinner
Respiration of malic acid speeds up as temperature rises.
“Sugar is there but tannins are still harsh” describes which problem?
A. Coulure
B. Phenolic ripeness lagging sugar
C. Noble rot
D. Spring frost
Warming makes this mismatch more common.
